rubric.why: Shows that class is the higher taxonomic rank and groups related orders.
rubric.description: Class is above order in classification and includes related orders.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the rank relationship or what a class contains.

rubric.why: Shows that order is below class and groups related families.
rubric.description: Order is below class in classification and includes related families.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the rank relationship or what an order contains.

modelAnswer: A class is a taxonomic rank above order and consists of related orders.
An order is below class and consists of related families.

rubric.why: Identifies diffusion as the movement of particles.
rubric.description: Diffusion is the movement of particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles move.

rubric.why: States the direction of movement that defines diffusion.
rubric.description: Particles move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct direction of movement.

modelAnswer: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

items.followUp: In which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and between which chromatids?

rubric.why: Identifies the exchange of chromosome material as crossing over.
rubric.description: Crossing over is the exchange of segments of genetic material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing an exchange of chromosome segments or genetic material.

rubric.why: Identifies the chromatids involved and/or the meiotic stage.
rubric.description: It occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the chromatids or stage.

modelAnswer: Crossing over is the exchange of segments of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
It occurs during prophase I of meiosis.

items.followUp: How does mitosis help repair damaged tissues?

rubric.why: Recognizes that mitosis produces new cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis forms new cells or daughter cells.

rubric.why: Connects the production of cells with growth and development.
rubric.description: The increased number of cells allows an organism to grow and develop.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking mitosis or increased cell number to growth or development.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells, increasing the number of cells in the body.
This increase in cell number enables growth and development.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a tissue cell and a gamete.

rubric.why: Identifies somatic cells as ordinary body cells.
rubric.description: Somatic cells are body cells and are not involved in producing gametes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing somatic cells.

rubric.why: Identifies germline cells with reproduction and gamete formation.
rubric.description: Germline cells are reproductive cells that give rise to gametes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing germline cells.

modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the non-reproductive cells that make up the body.
Germline cells are reproductive cells that give rise to gametes.

items.followUp: What is the difference between anabolism and catabolism?

rubric.why: Identifies metabolism as a set of chemical reactions.
rubric.description: Metabolism is the sum of chemical reactions in an organism or its cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining metabolism as chemical reactions in the organism or cells.

rubric.why: Shows that metabolism includes both kinds of reactions.
rubric.description: Metabolism includes anabolic and catabolic reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both anabolism and catabolism or describing building-up and breaking-down reactions.

modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions occurring in an organism or its cells.
It includes both building-up (anabolic) and breaking-down (catabolic) reactions.

items.followUp: What is a cofactor, and how does it help an enzyme?

rubric.why: Identifies a co-enzyme as an organic, non-protein molecule.
rubric.description: A co-enzyme is a small organic, non-protein molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a co-enzyme is organic and non-protein.

rubric.why: Explains the co-enzyme's role in enzyme action.
rubric.description: A co-enzyme associates with an enzyme and helps it carry out its function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it assists enzyme activity.

modelAnswer: A co-enzyme is a small organic, non-protein molecule.
It associates with an enzyme and helps the enzyme carry out its function.

items.followUp: How does carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: States the effect of increasing light intensity on photosynthesis.
rubric.description: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increased light intensity raises the rate.

rubric.why: Recognizes that the rate eventually stops increasing because another factor limits it.
rubric.description: At high light intensity the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the increase levels off or reaches a maximum.

modelAnswer: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases.
At high light intensity, the rate levels off because another factor becomes limiting.
